{{Short description|none}}
'''Japan had a substantial influence on Chinese culture''', particularly in the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Chalmers |date=1972 |title=How China and Japan See Each Other |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20037943 |journal=Foreign Affairs |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=711–721 |doi=10.2307/20037943 |issn=0015-7120 |jstor=20037943|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Japanese And Japan 's Influence On Chinese Culture {{!}} Bartleby |url=https://www.bartleby.com/essay/Japanese-And-Japan-s-Influence-On-Chinese-P38UTKTGXZQ |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=www.bartleby.com}}</ref> Though [[China–Japan relations|relations]] between Japan and [[China]] are historically fraught, the popularity of [[Japanese pop culture]] in China has been a means for easing tension.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wu |first=Yuqing |date=2021-08-05 |title=Can Pop Culture Allay Resentment? Japan's Influence in China Today |url=https://www.cogitatiopress.com/mediaandcommunication/article/view/4117 |journal=Media and Communication |language=en |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=112–122 |doi=10.17645/mac.v9i3.4117 |issn=2183-2439 |doi-access=free}}</ref> 

== Manhua ==
The word {{lang|zh-Latn|manhua}} was originally an 18th-century term used in Chinese [[literati painting]]. It became popular in Japan as ''[[manga]]'' in the late 19th century. [[Feng Zikai]] reintroduced the word to Chinese, in the modern sense, with his 1925 series of political cartoons, entitled ''Zikai Manhua,'' in ''Wenxue Zhoubao'' (Literature Weekly).<ref>{{cite book |last=Petersen |first=Robert S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hr7aZh6oonoC&pg=PA120 |title=Comics, Manga, and Graphic Novels: A History of Graphic Narratives |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2011 |isbn=9780313363306}}</ref><ref name="Lent">Lent, John A. [2001] (2001) Illustrating Asia: Comics, Humor Magazines, and Picture Books. University of Hawaii Press. {{ISBN|0-8248-2471-7}}</ref> While terms other than {{lang|zh-Latn|manhua}} had existed before, this publication took precedence over the many other descriptions for cartoon art, and {{lang|zh-Latn|manhua}} became a general term for all Chinese comic materials.<ref name="Wendy">Wong, Wendy Siuyi.  [2002] (2001) ''[[Hong Kong Comics: A History of Manhua]]''. [[Princeton Architectural Press]], New York.  {{ISBN|1-56898-269-0}}</ref>

== Animation ==
In 2011, Chinese company [[Vasoon Animation]] released ''[[Kuiba]]''. The film borrows from a Japanese "hot-blooded" style, refreshing the audience's views on Chinese animation. ''Kuiba'' was critically acclaimed; however, it commercially fell below expectations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chinese Animation at a Crossroads |url=http://english.cntv.cn/program/cultureexpress/20120312/108308.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130314025847/http://english.cntv.cn/program/cultureexpress/20120312/108308.shtml |archive-date=14 March 2013 |access-date=2012-10-30 |work=CNTV English}}</ref> It was reported that CEO Wu Hanqing received minority help from a venture capital fund at [[Tsinghua University]] to complete ''Kuiba''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kemp |first=Stuart |date=24 June 2011 |title=Beijing Calls the Toons |work=The Independent |location=London |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/screen-talk-beijing-calls-the-toon-2301735.html |access-date=2012-10-30}}</ref> This film holds distinction as the first big Chinese animation series to enter the Japanese market.<ref>{{cite web |title=China Animation To Be Screened in Japan Before Its Mainland Theater Release |url=http://china-screen-news.com/2011/06/china-animation-to-be-screened-in-japan-tv-before-its-mainland-theater-release/ |access-date=2012-10-30 |work=China Screen News |archive-date=2015-04-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402142315/http://china-screen-news.com/2011/06/china-animation-to-be-screened-in-japan-tv-before-its-mainland-theater-release/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
